claims.text: The as-sprayed CoCrFeMnNi bond coat has a heterogeneous microstructure.
The as-sprayed CoCrFeMnNi bond coat has relatively coarse grains and variable grain-boundary distributions.
A laser energy density of 0.5–1.5 kJ/cm² in argon is an appropriate remelting window for this bond coat.
Post-remelting stress-relief cooling mitigates residual-stress development.
Laser remelting rapidly melts and resolidifies the surface layer.
Optimized laser remelting refines and homogenizes the CoCrFeMnNi bond-coat microstructure.
Laser remelting reduces microstructural defects in the CoCrFeMnNi bond coat.
The remelted grain structure has fewer fast diffusion paths.
Stress-relief cooling minimizes residual stresses after laser remelting.
Microstructural refinement, defect reduction, and residual-stress mitigation promote a uniform and adherent passivating oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer reduces high-temperature degradation and spallation.
Treated bond coats will have a lower oxidation rate than untreated as-sprayed bond coats.
Treated bond coats will form a thinner and more uniform oxide scale than untreated bond coats.
Treated bond coats will exhibit less oxide spallation during cyclic high-temperature exposure.
The treatment will improve overall coating durability and reliability.
The improvement will remain effective during cyclic exposure at 1150–1200 °C when remelting is conducted in argon with controlled energy input and optimized cooling.
Performance may diminish if cooling does not adequately relieve stress or if the treatment is spatially nonuniform.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both oxidation rate and oxide spallation relative to the as-sprayed control would falsify the hypothesis.
Treatment-induced residual stress or microcracking that causes premature coating failure would falsify the hypothesis.
